query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition (approximately 1–2 atomic percent of Nb) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will lead to Nb segregation at the lamellar phase boundaries between the ductile L12 and brittle B2 phases, thereby enhancing interfacial cohesion and suppressing microcrack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries where microcrack initiation has been observed during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Incorporate 1–2 at.% Nb into the alloy during melting and casting, followed by standard thermo-mechanical processing that preserves the dual-phase lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing conditions using specimens produced under identical processing conditions except for the Nb addition.
generation.structural_mediator: Nb atoms segregate to the phase boundaries between the L12 (ductile) and B2 (brittle) phases, reducing the local interfacial free energy and enhancing cohesion.
generation.mechanism: The Nb microalloying facilitates atomic-scale modifications at the phase boundaries, making them more resistant to dislocation penetration and reducing stress concentration at the interfaces. This improved interfacial strength delays microcrack initiation and propagation, enabling a better balance between work hardening in the ductile phase and the overall load-bearing capacity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Nb-modified alloy is expected to show an increase in room-temperature tensile ductility (for example, an improvement by up to 30% in elongation to failure) along with a modest increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths (approximately 10–20% higher) due to enhanced dislocation storage and back-stress strengthening originating at the improved phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the conventional AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA produced by standard casting and thermo-mechanical processing, which features dual-phase lamellar colonies with brittle internal boundaries that promote microcrack initiation and limit room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected under room-temperature tensile deformation and within the regime where the lamellar spacing and dual-phase architecture are maintained. Exceeding the optimal Nb concentration or significantly altering the processing may lead to the formation of unwanted secondary phases that could decrease ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The precise concentration range for optimum Nb segregation and its influence on phase boundary chemistry require further investigation. There is also uncertainty regarding the balance between beneficial segregation and the potential for forming brittle Nb-rich compounds if the Nb content is too high.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples with identical processing: one set of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys containing 1–2 at.% Nb and one set of baseline alloys without Nb. Conduct microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM with EDX or atom probe tomography) to confirm Nb segregation at the phase boundaries. Perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sets to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility.
measurements: Fracture surface morphology (to assess microcrack initiation)
Chemical mapping of phase boundaries to verify Nb segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-modified alloys do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in both tensile ductility and strength compared to the baseline, or if chemical analyses fail to detect Nb segregation at the phase boundaries, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Multiphase alloys with heterogeneous microstructures demonstrate excellent combination of strength and ductility, making them attractive for myriad structural applications [,,]. Recently, eutectic high entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple solid solution phases have been the subject of extensive research due to their promise of overcoming the strength-ductility tradeoff seen in metals and conventional alloys [,,,,,,,]. The AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy represents a canonical example of an eutectic HEA with the lamellar arrangement of CoCrFe-rich L12 and AlNi-rich B2 phases [], which exhibit an excellent combination of strength and ductility at room temperature as well as exceptional strain hardening behavior that is largely retained up to 700 °C. Different processing routes have been utilized for achieving a wide range of microstructural features, resulting in outstanding mechanical properties and excellent corrosion resistance in these alloys. The ease of attaining ultrafine microstructure in directly cast eutectic HEAs is uncommon in conventional alloys []. Recently, new types of dual-phase high entropy alloys (HEAs) were designed under the inspiration of second phase strengthening, showing good combination of high fracture strength and tensile ductility at room temperature,. In contrast to the conventional strategies for alloy design, HEAs are developed with at least five metallic elements, emerging as a new frontier of research in recent years. The chemically disordered distributions of multiple elements in HEAs have been suggested to show important influence on dislocation slip,. In particularly, the high mixture of multiple elements in dual-phase HEAs may form distinctive phase boundary structures compared to conventional ones, which could result in different influence on dislocation behaviors. However, experimental observation and analysis are still lacking for a profound understanding of the deformation mechanisms of dual-phase HEAs.

Unlike microstructural heterogeneities, which have been investigated so far to achieve strength-ductility synergy in different materials,, including HEAs,,, the novel strategy developed in the present research leads to a different paradigm featured by dual structural-compositional heterogeneities. On the microstructural side, the heterogeneities are ensured by the presence of the LRs and NCRs, while on the compositional side it is featured by a number of different constituents. While the LRs consist of L12 and B2 (containing disordered nano-precipitates), the NCRs contain different ordered and disordered phases with differences in structure, composition and internal strain or defect densities. Evidently, the dual structural-compositional heterogeneities offer a large number of interfaces and boundaries separating widely different hardness domains and phases. The massive back-stress strengthening in such heterogeneous microstructural arrangements results in super-strong EHEA coupled with appreciable ductility. papers.title: Phase-Specific Damage Tolerance of a Eutectic High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with two-phase lamellar colonies (L12 and B2 phases)
papers.approach: Micro-cantilever bending experiments with notches milled in each phase and at phase boundaries to probe intrinsic fracture behavior.
papers.findings: The ductile L12 phase exhibited robust strain hardening and plastic deformation while the B2 phase showed limited damage tolerance with rapid crack initiation and propagation. This indicates the differing phase‐specific contributions toward overall mechanical performance.
papers.mechanism: Intrinsic differences in deformation mechanisms: L12 phase undergoes significant plasticity and strain hardening while the B2 phase is brittle and prone to micro‐cracking at internal boundaries.

papers.title: The Exceptional Strong Face-centered Cubic Phase and Semi-coherent Phase Boundary in a Eutectic Dual-phase High Entropy Alloy AlCoCrFeNi.
papers.system: Eutectic dual-phase HEA (AlCoCrFeNi) with FCC and BCC/B2 phases arranged in a lamellar structure
papers.approach: In situ deformation experiments combined with detailed microstructural and phase-boundary assessments.
papers.findings: Pre-straining of the FCC phase and the presence of strong, semi-coherent phase boundaries enhance overall strength without dramatically sacrificing ductility; the chemically disordered interfaces facilitate dislocation storage and delay failure.
papers.mechanism: Semi-coherent phase boundaries act as strong barriers to dislocation motion while the pre-strained FCC phase contributes via work hardening, collectively balancing strength and ductility.

papers.title: Enhanced strength-ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA retaining its composite lamellar microstructure
papers.approach: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing involving casting, rolling, and annealing designed to inherit and refine the lamellar structure to produce an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure.
papers.findings: Achieved a unique hierarchical microstructure that yields significantly improved yield strength and ductility compared to traditional processing routes; a self‐generated microcrack–arresting mechanism was observed.
papers.mechanism: Dual-hierarchical constraint: the retained lamellae create abundant interfaces that provide back-stress and impede crack propagation, while the ultrafine grain structure allows for enhanced strain hardening.

papers.title: Influence of ordered L1<sub>2</sub> precipitation on strain-rate dependent mechanical behavior in a eutectic high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic HEA featuring an FCC matrix with B2 phase components
papers.approach: Application of targeted heat treatments to induce ordered L12 nano-precipitates within the FCC phase; mechanical testing under quasi-static and dynamic loading.
papers.findings: The alloy exhibited a tensile yield strength close to 990 MPa and maintained reasonable ductility (~13%) under room-temperature conditions while displaying enhanced flow stresses at high strain rates.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via the formation of coherent L12 nano-precipitates in the ductile FCC matrix, which improves load transfer and delays the onset of localized deformation, while also promoting deformation twinning at higher strain rates.

papers.title: Small-scale mechanical behavior of a eutectic high entropy alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with a lamellar arrangement of L12 and B2 solid-solution phases
papers.approach: Nano-indentation and micro-pillar compression tests to probe phase-specific mechanical properties.
papers.findings: Observed dual yielding behavior: the L12 phase deformed in a homogeneous, slip-dominated manner (exhibiting ductile behavior) whereas the B2 phase deformed by plastic barreling but ultimately failed in a brittle manner. Mixed micro-pillars demonstrated that the interface between phases remained intact during deformation.
papers.mechanism: Intrinsic phase-specific dislocation behavior governs the mechanical responses, with the B2 phase showing higher hardness and strain rate sensitivity, while the FCC/L12 phase provides ductility through activation of multiple slip systems.

papers.title: Nanostructuring with Structural-Compositional Dual Heterogeneities Enhances Strength-Ductility Synergy in Eutectic High Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: A novel hybrid-rolling process combining cryo-rolling and warm-rolling to induce dual structural and compositional heterogeneities, producing regions of retained lamellae and transformed nanocrystalline domains.
papers.findings: The resultant dual heterogeneous microstructure achieved nanostructural domains with an unprecedented combination of strength (~2000 MPa) and ductility (~8%), attributed to a highly effective back-stress strengthening mechanism.
papers.mechanism: The coexistence of regions with distinct crystallographic and compositional characteristics offers a large number of phase boundaries and interfacial constraints, which work collectively to arrest crack propagation and promote strain hardening.

papers.title: Hierarchical Eutectoid Nano-lamellar Decomposition in an Al<sub>0.3</sub>CoFeNi Complex Concentrated Alloy.
papers.approach: Thermomechanical processing leading to a solid-state eutectoid decomposition of a single FCC phase into a nano-lamellar structure comprising FCC (or L12) and BCC (or B2) phases; subsequent annealing to tailor the microstructure.
papers.findings: The nano-lamellar microstructure could be tuned via annealing to yield either a high yield strength (~1074 MPa with 8% ductility) or a more damage-tolerant configuration (~900 MPa with >20% ductility), highlighting the tunability of properties based on processing conditions.
papers.mechanism: A two-step decomposition process—first, the formation of coarse lamellar colonies by eutectoid reaction, and then a secondary ordering transformation within lamellae—results in an interplay between ordering-induced strengthening and interface effectiveness.

established: Eutectic HEAs typically feature dual-phase lamellar microstructures with a soft, ductile FCC/L12 phase and a hard, brittle B2 phase.
The intrinsic mechanical responses of the two phases differ, with ductility largely provided by the L12 phase and strength contributed by both phases through interface strengthening.
Conventional processing methods often enhance strength at the expense of ductility because of microcrack formation at internal boundaries.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermo-mechanical processing (casting, rolling, annealing) to inherit and refine the lamellar microstructure
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved ultrafine-grained duplex structures that significantly improved the yield strength while retaining or enhancing ductility.

approaches_tried.approach: Targeted heat treatments to induce coherent ordered L12 nano-precipitates in the FCC matrix
approaches_tried.outcome: Resulted in precipitation strengthening that maintained ductility under both quasi-static and dynamic loading conditions.

approaches_tried.approach: Hybrid cryo-rolling and warm-rolling to generate dual structural and compositional heterogeneities
approaches_tried.outcome: Produced a microstructure with enhanced interfacial density and back-stress strengthening that significantly improved both strength and ductility.

mechanisms: Differential phase deformation: Ductility via the FCC/L12 phase and brittleness via the B2 phase.
Strengthening by phase boundaries: Semi-coherent boundaries and chemically disordered interfaces impede dislocation motion.
Precipitation strengthening: Formation of coherent L12 nano-precipitates enhances load transfer.
Back-stress and strain gradient effects arising from heterogeneous microstructural domains.
disagreements: While some studies emphasize the role of the hard B2 phase as a primary contributor to strength (despite its brittleness), others argue that pre-straining and strengthening of the FCC/L12 phase is equally or more important.
There is debate over whether microcrack initiation is predominantly driven by inherent brittleness of the B2 phase or by stress concentrations at the phase boundaries.
open_questions: What single, targeted intervention can simultaneously suppress microcrack nucleation (thus enhancing ductility) while reinforcing the overall strength of lamellar eutectic HEAs?
How can the interfacial chemistry and coherence be optimized to avoid the trade-off between strength and ductility?
What are the precise boundary conditions (e.g., strain rate, temperature) under which modifications to the phase boundary architecture lead to improved room-temperature mechanical performance?
How generalizable are the mechanisms observed in AlCoCrFeNi2.1-type systems to other eutectic HEA compositions?
opportunities: Develop a single intervention that targets the phase boundaries—e.g., engineering the interfacial chemistry via controlled precipitation or alloying additions—which could enhance phase boundary cohesion and arrest microcrack propagation.
Explore processing routes that promote coherent nanoprecipitation on the interfaces, simultaneously boosting dislocation storage in ductile phases and resisting crack propagation in brittle regions.

Combine thermo-mechanical processing with in situ chemical modifications to tailor interfacial structures, possibly using minor additions that segregate to phase boundaries to lower their energy and improve ductility.

Design experiments focused on systematically varying interfacial characteristics (such as coherency and chemical disorder) to directly assess their impact on both strength and tensile ductility at room temperature.

directions.assessment: By adding a minor alloying element that segregates to the phase boundaries, this approach directly targets the weak interfaces that otherwise serve as crack nucleation sites. It is supported by studies showing that chemically disordered and semi‐coherent boundaries can be strengthened either by solute segregation or controlled precipitation (e.g., PMC10743261, PMC6175879, PMC6687781). This method is a single, targeted intervention and is feasible with standard casting and thermal processing.

directions.direction: Tailored aging to induce coherent nanoprecipitates at interfaces
directions.type: heat or thermomechanical treatment and microstructure control
directions.assessment: Using a controlled post-solidification heat treatment to generate coherent nano‐scale precipitates at or near phase boundaries could enhance both strength (through precipitation hardening) and ductility (by impeding microcrack propagation). However, precise control over precipitate size and distribution is challenging.

directions.direction: Hybrid cryo-rolling and warm-rolling to create dual structural-compositional heterogeneities
directions.assessment: This process introduces significant microstructural refinement and interfacial density improvements that have been shown to boost strength and ductility (PMC6687781). However, it is a multi-step process and may not be considered a single intervention.

directions.direction: Severe plastic deformation followed by rapid annealing to refine lamellar spacing
directions.assessment: While further refining the lamellar colony can improve back-stress effects and delay crack coalescence, this approach risks additional microcrack formation if the internal interfaces are not intrinsically strengthened.

directions.direction: Surface modification treatments (e.g., coating) to mitigate microcrack nucleation at boundaries
directions.assessment: Surface coatings can shield external crack nucleation but do not address the intrinsic weakness of the internal phase boundaries. This makes them less directly effective against the microstructural brittleness observed.

choice.why: This intervention directly targets the phase boundary weakness that initiates microcracking, by promoting beneficial solute segregation which enhances interfacial cohesion. It is a single, targeted change that aligns with observed improvements in phase boundary strength and dislocation storage, and it can be implemented without overhauling the established lamellar structure.
